::: {#sol-dropout-run}

```{python}
#| code-fold: show
drop_net = make_net(p_drop=0.5)
drop_history, _ = fit(drop_net)
drop_best_val = drop_history["val"].min()
drop_final_val = drop_history["val"].iloc[-1]
print(drop_best_val, best_val_loss, drop_final_val, final_row["val"])
```

With [dropout](#def-dropout) the lowest validation loss is `r sprintf("%.3f", py$drop_best_val)`,
against `r sprintf("%.3f", py$best_val_loss)` without it,
and the final one is `r sprintf("%.3f", py$drop_final_val)`,
against `r sprintf("%.3f", py$final_row[["val"]])`.
On this small problem,
trained on all `r py$n_train` images at every step,
dropout changes the validation loss little,
and the [weight decay](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/regularization.html#def-weight-decay) of @sol-weight-decay-sweep does far more.
How much a regularizer helps depends on the network and the data,
which is why the [validation set](https://morrison-lab.github.io/lds/chapters/big-ideas.html#def-validation-set) decides.

:::
